saints.name: Peter the Aleut
saints.dates: Early nineteenth century;1815 in the historical Orthodox America account

summary.text: Peter is commemorated as an Indigenous Orthodox martyr in California. The OCA preserves the account transmitted by Simeon Yanovsky to Saint Herman, while acknowledging that little is known about Peter’s wider life.

blocks.text: The source identifies him as from Kodiak but does not supply a family history or surname. Yanovsky reports hearing the events from Peter’s imprisoned companion. Thus the published account contains an explicit chain of testimony, rather than a surviving first-person autobiography by Peter.

blocks.text: In the received account, fourteen Aleuts are imprisoned in California and pressed to accept Catholicism. Peter refuses. The OCA text corrects the transmitted designation Jesuits to Franciscans; the source itself therefore signals a problem in the reported institutional identification. His companion survives when an order arrives requiring the prisoners’ release and transfer to Monterey.

blocks.text: Christopher Orr’s 2011 guest article distinguishes historical questions from the development of veneration and ecclesiastical recognition. It refers readers to the earlier 1981 Orthodox Life discussion and Michael Kovach’s 1957 thesis as research leads. Orr argues that sparse frontier documentation must be assessed in its setting and that lack of documentation alone does not prove nonexistence. He also distinguishes uncertainty about specific stories from the Church’s recognition of sanctity. These are a named contributor’s historical and ecclesiological arguments; they are not presented as a council’s determination or as a new conclusion by this app.

blocks.text: Yanovsky says he reported the incident to Saint Petersburg. He then recounts Herman asking the martyr’s name and immediately addressing Peter as a holy new martyr before an icon.

blocks.text: The account describes progressive cutting of fingers and limbs, and death from blood loss while he continues confessing Christ. This specific death method is attributed to the transmitted witness story.

blocks.text: Abbot Herman’s article places Peter alongside Hieromonk Juvenal as an early martyr of Orthodoxy in America. It gives San Francisco and 1815 for Peter’s death and connects later recognition with the service prepared for Herman’s 1970 glorification. The article explains that the absence of a separate formal glorification had contributed to neglect, then notes a subsequent episcopal decree. Its discussion reflects the historical Russian Church Abroad setting of the publication. Its broader polemical character is retained in the source description rather than converted into an app-written judgment about another communion.

blocks.text: Orr reproduces a 1980 ROCOR decree as an addendum. The published decree says a new canonization decision is unnecessary because their names already appear in Herman’s service; this is a document reported within a later article.

blocks.text: Orr asks how local veneration developed before the1970s and which primary sources informed Herman’s service.
